title: Basic Security and Identifying User Types

sections.title: Mission · Identify Users and Privileges
paragraphs: Linux is a multi-user operating system. Different users can have different identities, privileges, files, groups, and responsibilities. Distinguish root, standard users, and system users, then recognize the files and commands for accounts, groups, logins, and privilege changes.

sections.title: Linux Is a Multi-User System
paragraphs: Linux separates user identities so the system can decide who owns resources and what each account may do. Users can belong to groups and receive different permissions.

sections.title: Standard Users
paragraphs: A standard user is a normal daily account with limited authority. It should not have unrestricted administrative control by default.

sections.title: root
paragraphs: root is the Linux superuser with broad administrative authority. Root can change system configuration, manage accounts, and access protected resources.

sections.title: Root Security Principle
paragraphs: Powerful administrative access increases risk. Use elevated privileges only when needed and return to ordinary privileges afterward.
sections.callout: USE ADMINISTRATIVE PRIVILEGES ONLY WHEN NEEDED

sections.title: System Users
paragraphs: A system user is an account created mainly for a service, daemon, or background process rather than an interactive human session.
sections.callout: SYSTEM USER = ACCOUNT FOR A SERVICE OR PROCESS

table.caption: Match the account to its role

sections.title: /etc/passwd
paragraphs: /etc/passwd stores general user account information such as usernames, numeric IDs, home directories, and login shells. Modern systems do not normally store password hashes there.

sections.title: /etc/shadow
paragraphs: /etc/shadow stores protected password-hash and password-aging information and is more tightly restricted.

sections.title: Exam Trap · passwd vs. shadow
paragraphs: /etc/passwd answers who the user is. /etc/shadow protects sensitive authentication and password-aging data.

sections.title: /etc/group
paragraphs: /etc/group stores group definitions and membership information.

sections.title: id
paragraphs: id displays identity details such as the user ID, primary group, and supplementary group memberships.
sections.callout: id = WHO AM I AND WHAT GROUPS AM I IN?

sections.title: who
paragraphs: who displays users currently logged in.

sections.title: w
paragraphs: w displays logged-in users plus information about what they are doing and system activity.
sections.callout: w = WHO IS HERE + WHAT ARE THEY DOING?

sections.title: Exam Trap · who vs. w
paragraphs: who focuses on who is logged in. w adds user activity information.

sections.title: last
paragraphs: last displays login history, showing previous user sessions.

sections.title: sudo
paragraphs: sudo runs an authorized command with elevated authority according to policy.

sections.title: su
paragraphs: su switches to another user identity, often opening a shell as that user when authorized. If no username is supplied, su targets root by default.
sections.callout: SU USER = SWITCH TO THAT USER · SU ALONE = ROOT BY DEFAULT

sections.title: Exam Trap · sudo vs. su
paragraphs: sudo elevates a command. su switches or becomes another user.

sections.title: GSA Scenario Recognition
bullets: Account for a background service → System user
Switch to a named user → su USER
Start a root shell by default → su with no username

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: System user → Service or process account
sections.callout: ROOT SUPERUSER · STANDARD EVERYDAY · SYSTEM SERVICE · ID IDENTITY · WHO CURRENT · W ACTIVITY · LAST HISTORY · SUDO ELEVATE · SU SWITCH
